coverage_note: § 1 and § 3 (lines 27-58 and 97-148): the paragraphs carrying fulfilment vocabulary. Not read: §§ 10, 37, 41, 49, 50 and 51 (4-10 hits each, mostly in very long sections) and the rest of the commentary.

units.claim: Henry's summary of Husserl has signifying intentions find a fulfillment that can reach the living presence of the thing, and the way this fulfillment operates defines the degree of evidence.
units.quote: Henry continues: the way in which this fulfillment operates defines the degree of the evidence.

units.claim: At the highest degree of perfection is an originary evidence in which all elements of the signifying intention are fulfilled by a corresponding intuition, but it is perfect only if it cannot be belied by later experience.
units.quote: at the highest degree of perfection, we find an immediate, originary evidence in which the diverse elements of signifying intention by which consciousness aims at the object are all fulfilled by a corresponding intuition

units.claim: The ego becomes the theme of a consciousness seeking apodicticity only because it alone can furnish an adequate intuitive fulfillment.
units.quote: The ego arises before it only because it is the sole being capable of furnishing to such a consciousness an adequate intuitive fulfillment.

units.claim: Three senses of intuition are distinguished: every presenting act, a consciousness whose signifying intentions are fulfilled, and the fulfilling given itself.
units.quote: (3) The fulfillment itself of intuition, understood as the arising of a given to which the signifying intentions of consciousness come to adjoin themselves in a rigorous correspondence.

units.claim: The content that gives fulfillment the occasion to occur remains the true goal of intentional life, which is why rational life stays oriented by being-there.
units.quote: the content that must give this fulfillment the occasion to be produced — which remains the true goal of intentional life

units.claim: The ideal of a consciousness whose signifying intentions are all intuitively realized is questioned as a dangerous ideal in which forgetting of the origin is engendered.
units.quote: is it not, however, in many respects, and despite its practical fecundity, a dangerous ideal? Is it not in this ideal that originary forgetting is engendered, the forgetting of the origin and of the foundation?

units.claim: The commentary states that if the horizon of unfulfilled co-intentions belongs to consciousness in principle, it is a positive ontological structure, not a deficit of intuition.
units.quote: But if the horizon belongs to consciousness *in principle*, then the horizon is not a deficit of intuition but a positive ontological structure — and the ideal of total intuition is a deceptive, even "dangerous" ideal.

units.claim: Husserl's horizon-doctrine is said to serve only to describe how the not-yet-fulfilled content converts into the fulfilled given, so that the essence of the horizon as such is missed.
units.quote: it uses the doctrine of the horizon as an auxiliary device to describe how the content *within* the horizon (the not-yet-fulfilled) is supposed to convert itself into the content *at the center* of the horizon (the fulfilled given).

units.claim: Henry proposes beginning not from fulfilled intuition but from the confused, non-intuitive consciousness before fulfillment, still immersed in the horizon.
units.quote: Henry proposes beginning from the confused, non-intuitive consciousness — the consciousness before fulfillment, still immersed in the horizon as such.
